title: The card you write while you are calm
summary: A light hour on purpose. Write your own pre-contest protocol card from your own half crossing debrief, tidy the Error Bestiary without a line of new C++, prove the grader account still works, and set the kit out for Saturday's crossing.
materials: one stiff index card and a pen that does not smudge
your half crossing debrief page from week 5
the analog desk clock, and no phone on the desk
the Error Bestiary notebook opened in week 1
laptop with Python and your own usaco.org account
the bug diary and the maker's log

steps.title: Ask, imagine, plan
steps.body:
The design loop, same six moves: ask, imagine, plan, build, test, fix. Today the thing being built is a piece of paper, and it is still a build.

Ask: what does the version of you sitting down at dawn on Saturday need, that the version of you sitting here right now is able to give them? They will be somewhere you are not. They will have three problems they have never seen, a clock they started themselves, and nobody to ask. They will also be, at some point in that morning, tired and stuck and fairly sure that pushing harder is the answer. You are none of those things today. That asymmetry is the whole reason this hour exists.

Imagine: one card on the desk beside the clock. Not a page, not a notebook, a card, because a card gets read and a page gets ignored. Every line on it is something you can actually do with your hands, and every line got there because something on the half crossing put it there.

Plan: three jobs, in this order. Write the card. Tidy the Bestiary shelf and prove the tools still work. Set out the kit and check one fact about the contest you picked that will otherwise cost you an hour.

And the thing this week says out loud rather than quietly doing: this week is light on purpose, in all three tracks, and it is the lightest week of the season. Not because there is nothing left to teach, but because you do not walk into a long morning already tired. Nothing new in C++ goes in front of you this week. Doing less right now is part of the work, not a hole in it. That is a hard sentence to believe at this age, so here is the test: after Saturday, look at your own pace page and decide for yourself whether it was true.

Five minutes, and today it is Python, because Saturday is Python.

Drill the two input shapes, because you will use exactly one of them and you will not know which until you open the problem page.

Shape one, the file shape, used by the contests before December 2020. The problem page names the files itself.

    with open("prob.in") as f:
        data = f.read().split()

    with open("prob.out", "w") as f:
        f.write(str(answer) + "\n")

Shape two, the terminal shape, used from the December 2020 contest onwards.

    import sys
    data = sys.stdin.read().split()
    print(answer)

Type each block five times without looking down. On the day, prob gets replaced by the short name the problem page gives, exactly as it is spelled there.

Then thirty seconds on the punctuation that breaks Python rather than C++: the colon at the end of a with line, the quotes around a file name, and the four spaces of indent underneath. A stray indent is a whole minute you did not plan to spend.

figure.alt: Attention on a long, unbroken task, drawn as a line that falls fast in the first half hour and then levels off lower down. Most of the drop happens early; after that the line stays low rather than continuing to fall, which is why parking a problem and coming back later helps more than pushing straight through.

steps.title: Attention is a budget, and it is not the same budget all morning
steps.body:
You already treat time as a budget. Today, the other budget.

Here is a finding that is about eighty years old, first measured in 1948, and repeated in laboratories ever since. Sit somebody in front of a display and ask them to watch for a rare, quiet signal, the way a radar operator does. Their catch rate does not stay flat. It drops, measurably, and most of the drop has already happened inside the first half hour. Researchers call it the vigilance decrement. The size of the drop varies a lot between one task and another and between one person and another, so nobody can hand you your own number. What is solid is the shape: attention on a long, unbroken, low-variety task goes down, not sideways.

Second thing, and this one you can feel. Read back something you wrote yourself, immediately, hunting for mistakes, and you will miss things a stranger would catch on the first pass. You are not reading the page. You are reading what you meant, from memory, and the page is just a prompt for it. Leave it and come back, and the memory has faded enough for the page to be visible again. That is what fresh eyes actually are. Not extra cleverness, and not a better mood. It is your own memory of what you intended getting quieter.

That is the whole mechanism behind parking a problem. When you are stuck, the reason is often that you have a wrong idea about the problem and you cannot see it, because you are reading your idea instead of the words. Fifteen minutes on a different problem does not make you smarter. It makes the wrong idea quieter, and when you come back the sentence you skated over is suddenly there.

One honest warning about the science, because it matters more than the science. There is a very popular story that attention runs on fuel, that willpower is a tank that empties, and that sugar refills it. That story had a rough decade: careful attempts to reproduce the headline experiments often did not, and the field is still arguing. Do not build your card on it. Build your card on the two things above, which are old, boring and repeatedly measured, and on the only dataset that is genuinely about you: your own pace page from the half crossing.

figure.alt: The elbow as a pulling pair: the biceps in front bunches up and pulls to bend the elbow while the triceps behind goes slack, then the reverse happens to straighten it, the triceps pulling while the biceps relaxes. A muscle only ever pulls, never pushes, so every joint that bends both ways needs one muscle for each direction.

steps.title: Muscles only pull, so they always come in pairs
steps.body:
Your legs are about to do real work on Saturday's crossing, so it is worth knowing what a muscle can and cannot do. A muscle only ever pulls. It contracts and shortens, and that is its one move. It cannot push itself back out again.

That is exactly the limit of a servo winding in a string: strong pulling one way, nothing the other way. So your body, like a robot built only from pulling parts, wires muscles in opposing pairs. Bend your elbow and the biceps pulls while the triceps relaxes. Straighten it and the triceps pulls while the biceps relaxes. Neither one ever pushes.

Every joint that bends both ways runs on this same pairing trick, one muscle for each direction, never a single muscle doing both jobs.

Feel it yourself: grip your upper arm and slowly bend your elbow. The front muscle bunches up while the back one goes slack, then the reverse on the way down.

steps.title: Write the card, and write it yourself
steps.body:
One index card. One side if it fits, both if it does not. Handwritten, by you, and nobody else writes a line on it. A parent may ask you a question about it. A parent may not answer one.

Open your half crossing debrief from week 5 first and read it all the way through before you write anything. Whatever is on it, that page is the only evidence you have about how you actually work under a clock, and evidence beats advice. Every line on the card has to be traceable back to something that really happened that morning, or to something you noticed while it was happening. A line you copied from somebody's advice is somebody else's card.

The card is a set of answers, and here are the questions it has to answer. The questions are the format. The answers are entirely yours.

One. What do I do in the first ten minutes, before the editor is open at all?

Two. How do I choose which problem gets the next stretch of my time?

Three. What exactly do I check before I press submit? Name the checks, not the feeling.

Four. When do I park a problem, and what is the number that tells me? A number means a count of minutes or a count of failed attempts, something the clock or the screen can tell you. Without a number, parking never happens, because the moment always feels like the wrong moment.

Five. What do I do when I come back to a parked problem? First move, in words.

Six. What is my break rule? When, how long, and what I do in the break.

Seven. What happens at minute two hundred, with most of your window behind you? By then the shape of the morning is decided and the useful moves are different from the ones at minute twenty.

Two rules about the writing itself. Every line has to be a thing you can do with your hands: read, draw, run, open, close, stand up, write down. Cross out anything that is a mood, because focus more and stay calm are not instructions, they are wishes. And keep it short enough that a tired person will actually read it. A card with fourteen lines is a card nobody reads at minute two hundred.

Write version one at the top. It is version one because it is going to be wrong somewhere, and the oasis is where you find out where.
checklist: The card is handwritten by me, on one card, nobody else wrote a line on it, and it says version one at the top
I read my week 5 debrief page end to end before writing anything on the card
Every line on the card is an action I could do with my hands, and every mood word got crossed out
The parking rule has an actual number in it that the clock or the screen can tell me
The card answers all seven questions and is still short enough to read in one glance

steps.title: Prove the tools, tidy the shelf, set out the kit
steps.body:
Three small jobs, none of which is new material, all of which are cheaper today than at dawn on Saturday.

Prove the tools. Log in to your own grader account. Take a problem you have already solved, submit the solution you already have, and watch the verdict screen come back. That is not practice at solving. It is proof that the account works, the browser works, the submit box is where you remember it and nothing about the site has changed since the last time you looked. Before you press submit, say out loud what you expect the screen to say. Then look. Doing that once today is worth more than doing it for the first time on Saturday.

Check the one fact that costs an hour if you get it wrong, and check it without spoiling Saturday. Do not open any problem from the contest you picked. Those three stories have to be new to you on the morning, and one read now is one fewer then. Instead, write down the date of the contest you picked, and then open a problem from a contest you have already done and read its INPUT FORMAT heading. There are two kinds, and the date decides which. Before December 2020 the heading names a file, in the shape INPUT FORMAT (file lostcow.in), with an OUTPUT FORMAT heading naming the matching .out file. Your program has to open exactly those names and write exactly that file. From the December 2020 contest onwards the heading names the terminal instead, in the shape INPUT FORMAT (input arrives from the terminal / stdin). Then the input comes in on standard input and you print the answer. So the date of your contest tells you which shape Saturday will be, and on the morning the problem page in front of you is the final authority. Not this page, not your memory, and not the last problem you happened to do. A perfectly correct program that reads the wrong place scores nothing at all, and the grader will not tell you that is why. Write the date and the shape on the back of your card.

Tidy the shelf. Read the Error Bestiary from the beginning. Add nothing new, because nothing new happened this week. Instead, put a mark beside every entry you now see coming before the compiler says it, and count the marks. That count is the only number you will get this week and it is not a score of you, it is a measurement of how far the shelf has already been walked.

Then set the kit out on the desk where it will sit: the card, the analog clock, blank paper, a pencil, water. No phone on the desk.
checklist: I submitted a solution I already own and watched a verdict come back on my own account
I said out loud what verdict I expected before I pressed submit, and then compared
I wrote my contest's date and its input shape on the back of my card, and I did not open any of its three problems
I read the Bestiary end to end, added nothing, and counted the entries I now see coming
The kit is out on the desk, the phone is not, and the clock is on the desk and working

steps.title: Saturday: the first full crossing
steps.body:
The date is already on the wall map, under the second sun, in your handwriting, because you chose it. That is all the map has to say about it. The map carries dates and never anything that shrinks.

What it is. One complete past Bronze contest from the archive, whichever one you picked. Three problems. The whole window that contest ran for, and the window belongs to the contest rather than to Bronze: December, January and February contests run four hours, and the US Open runs five. Look up which one you picked and write its hours at the top of your route page before Saturday. Python. Alone, at the dawn you named.

How it runs. The site does not put a clock on a past contest, because that contest ended years ago. So the clock is yours. Write the start time on the top of your route page, start the analog clock, and open the first problem. When your window is up, stop, and stop even if you are mid-sentence, because the stopping is a thing you are practising too.

Breaks are at your call, as many as your card says, and the clock keeps running through them. That is what a real window does and it is the whole reason a break has to be a decision rather than a drift.

The proctor stands at the door. That is a job with an exact description: they do not read the problems, they do not answer a question about a problem, they do not look at your screen and make a face. They refill the water and they make sure the house leaves you alone. If you ask them something about a problem, the correct answer from them is a shrug, and they should know that before Saturday starts.

The route page beside you, all morning. Every time something happens, write the clock time next to it in the margin. Started reading. Started problem two. Submitted. Wrong answer, went back to the paper. Stood up. Those times are the actual data of the morning, and at the oasis you will chart them and find out where your time really went, which is almost never where it felt like it went. If you do not write the times down at the time, they are gone, and there is no way to get them back afterwards.

Things that are true and worth knowing before you start. The grader takes as many submissions as you want on a past problem, so submitting early and being told no is a legal move and often a good one. A verdict of no is information, not a verdict on you. And you do not open anybody's solution or the published analysis until after the debrief, not once, no matter how much you want to. Reading the answer before you have written your own account of the morning wrecks the account, because you will write it as somebody who already knew.

The debrief happens the next day, not the same day. Route, weather, one pack item, exactly the form you learned in week 3, and no score anywhere in it. How many problems the grader accepted is not the report and does not belong in it. A morning honestly spent and honestly written up is a summit reached, and a rejection you understood by the end is a summit reached in weather.

steps.title: The bug diary on a week with almost no code
steps.body:
There is barely any code this week, so the diary gets a different kind of entry, and it is the one this season keeps circling.

Write down the prediction you made before the dry run submission, and then what the screen actually said. If they matched, write down why you were confident and whether the confidence was earned or lucky. If they did not match, that is the better entry, and it goes in with what you now think was really going on.

That is the mirage practised in miniature. Being sure a program is right and being right about a program are two different states, they feel exactly the same from the inside, and the only thing that can tell them apart is checking against something outside your own head. The grader is that outside thing. So is a sample test. So is a person you explain it to.

Then one line at the bottom, for the version of you reading this in a year: what you expect to be the hardest single minute of Saturday morning, and what your card says to do in it. On Sunday, come back and write underneath whether you were right about which minute it would be. That comparison is worth more than either answer on its own.

steps.title: Show it
steps.prompt: A photo of the protocol card, version one, both sides if you used both, close enough to read every line. Then the verdict screen from the dry run submission, with your written prediction beside it. Then, after Sunday, a photo of the route page from the crossing with the clock times in the margin, and the debrief written in the week 3 form.
